title: The replication crisis
hookLine: in 2015 only about 36 percent of a hundred psychology studies replicated clearly (Open Science Collaboration)

cards: A hundred psychology studies, already published in respected journals, were run a second time. Same questions, same methods, as close as the new teams could get, often with help from the original authors.
Nearly all the originals had reported a clear result. The repeats? About 36 percent did.
That came from a large group of researchers calling themselves the Open Science Collaboration. This path has spent weeks sharing findings from labs, so it owes you this part too.
A new section starts today: the honest part.

teach.b: First, what was done. The point wasn't to catch anyone out. It was a plain question: if you do the same study again, do you get the same answer?
The teams repeated each study once, carefully, and published everything, including the misses. Second, what came back.

teach.h: ABOUT A THIRD HELD UP CLEARLY.
teach.b: Only about a third of the repeats showed a clear result, and where an effect did show up again, it was often smaller than first reported. Third, what that does and doesn't mean.
A failed repeat doesn't prove the original was wrong, and it certainly doesn't prove anyone cheated. A single repeat can miss too.

teach.h: ONE STUDY IS A FIRST WORD.
teach.b: What it means is humbler: one study is a first word, not a last word. A finding earns trust by surviving being done again, by other people, in other places. Fourth, an old line that already knew this.
The book of Proverbs, in the King James text, says: "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him." The first account tends to sound right.
Then the neighbor arrives and checks.
Replication is the neighbor. And it applies here: many findings this path has shared were single studies, and a few came with a note that later work was mixed. That's no reason to throw them out.
It's a reason to hold them like any first account: with interest, and a question ready.

how: Researchers check a finding by running the same study again, often with new teams and larger groups; a result that holds up across repeats is trusted more than a single striking study.

o: when repeated studies came back weaker, or didn't come back at all
a funding shortage that stopped labs from running new studies
a scandal where many researchers were caught faking their data

games.q: a friend tells you about one striking new study. what do you do?
o: share it right away; it's published.
find it interesting, and ask whether it's been repeated.
games.why: the project's lesson is the middle way: a single study is worth hearing, and worth checking. a finding earns trust by surviving being done again.

practice: Bring to mind one finding you've taken on board, from this path, a headline or a friend: phones make us dumber, gratitude makes us happier, whatever comes. Hold it for a few breaths and ask quietly: was it repeated?
If you don't know, let the not-knowing sit beside the finding without pushing either one away.

wordCard.voice: The replication crisis. When psychology repeated its own studies, many results came back weaker or didn't come back at all. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: was it repeated? It's a kind question, not a cynical one. I'll be here tomorrow.
